Q1458409.t: Where the rivers of northern Karelia gather
Q1458409.s: Its name is usually read as 'main lake', and Pyaozero earns it: rivers from the forested hills pour in from all sides, among them the Olanga from Paanajärvi National Park. The water then leaves by the Kuma and travels on to the White Sea. In 1966 a dam raised the level, and the lake became part of the Kumskoye Reservoir. The Arctic Circle runs only about 60 km to the north.
Q1458409.w: A large, ragged lake full of islands and bays in dark forest, just south of the Arctic Circle and west of the White Sea.
f: Its open water covers about 659 km², not counting the islands.
Water leaving by the Kuma reaches the White Sea through Kovdozero and the Kovda River.
Topozero, to the south, drains into Pyaozero by the Sofyanga River.

q.q: Which sea does Pyaozero's water eventually reach?

Q1247231.t: The largest lake wholly inside New York State
Q1247231.s: Lake Champlain and the Great Lakes are bigger, but New York shares them; Oneida is the largest lake that lies entirely within the state. It is long and surprisingly shallow — about 34 km from end to end, yet on average only some 7 m deep — so a strong wind quickly whips up steep waves. The modern Erie Canal route runs straight across it.
Q1247231.w: A long, pale-blue lake lying east–west, just north-east of the sprawl of Syracuse.
f: Boats on the Erie Canal enter the lake at Sylvan Beach in the east and leave it at Brewerton in the west.
In winter the lake usually freezes over and fills with ice-fishing shanties.
It is named after the Oneida, one of the six nations of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy.

q.q: Which canal's modern route runs across Oneida Lake?

Q1335725.t: The Y-shaped Finger Lake with a flying past
Q1335725.s: All the other Finger Lakes are straight blades of water; only Keuka forks, and from the air it looks like a slightly crooked letter Y — early settlers simply called it Crooked Lake. At its southern tip lies Hammondsport, home town of the aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss. In 1908 his June Bug made the first publicly announced aeroplane flight in America there.
Q1335725.w: A forked, Y-shaped lake among long parallel lakes, just west of the much longer, straight Seneca Lake.
f: Keuka drains into Seneca Lake through a short outlet stream that drops about 80 m on the way.
Glenn Curtiss was born in Hammondsport in 1878 and built engines and aircraft there.
The steep slopes around the lake are at the heart of the Finger Lakes wine region.

q.q: What shape sets Keuka apart from the other Finger Lakes?

Q1552706.t: The deepest Finger Lake, its floor below sea level
Q1552706.s: Glaciers gouged the Finger Lakes like claw marks, and Seneca is the deepest scratch of all: about 188 m. Its surface lies roughly 136 m above sea level, so the bottom of this inland lake sits well below the level of the ocean. With so much water, it cools slowly and almost never freezes over, even in hard upstate winters.
Q1552706.w: A long, narrow north–south lake at the centre of the Finger Lakes, with Geneva at its northern end.
f: The lake is about 60 km long but nowhere much more than 5 km wide.
Watkins Glen, at its southern tip, is famous for a narrow gorge with 19 waterfalls.
Seneca holds more water than any other Finger Lake.

q.q: Roughly how deep is Seneca Lake at its deepest point?

Q731175.t: The longest Finger Lake, with Ithaca at its tip
Q731175.s: At about 61 km, Cayuga is the longest of the Finger Lakes — a slim blue line you can follow almost from end to end on a clear day. Ithaca and Cornell University sit at its southern tip, where gorges cut down through the hills. At the flat northern end the lake melts into the Montezuma marshes, a major stop for migrating geese and ducks.
Q731175.w: The longest lake of the group, running north–south just east of Seneca Lake, with Ithaca at its southern end.
f: Taughannock Falls, near the west shore, drops about 65 m — higher than Niagara Falls.
At some 133 m deep, Cayuga's floor also lies below sea level.
A canal links Cayuga to Seneca Lake, its neighbour to the west.

q.q: Which university stands at the southern end of Cayuga Lake?

Q945023.t: A wild lake on the sandstone of the Athabasca Basin
Q945023.s: Cree Lake spreads across about 1,435 km² of northern Saskatchewan, a maze of islands and bays in unbroken boreal forest. It lies almost wholly within the Athabasca Basin, a vast bowl of ancient sandstone that also hides the world's richest uranium ore. Its water leaves northward by the Cree River and, lake by lake, finds its way to Lake Athabasca.
Q945023.w: A big, island-studded lake in continuous dark forest, about 200 km south of Lake Athabasca.
f: At about 1,435 km², it is the fourth-largest lake in Saskatchewan.
The Cree River carries its water north to Black Lake, which drains into Lake Athabasca.
The Athabasca Basin holds the highest-grade uranium deposits known anywhere.

q.q: Which way does water leave Cree Lake?

Q719538.t: Source of the Kazan, near Canada's 'four corners'
Q719538.s: Only a few dozen kilometres to the south is the one point in Canada where four provinces and territories meet: Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nunavut and the Northwest Territories, at 60° N, 102° W. Kasba Lake itself is the source of the Kazan River, which runs about 1,000 km north to Baker Lake. Here the spruce forest is already thinning towards the tundra.
Q719538.w: A large, many-armed lake in sparse spruce forest, just north of the point where four Canadian provinces and territories meet.
f: The lake covers about 1,341 km²; most of it is in the Northwest Territories, a small part in Nunavut.
The Kazan River flows from Kasba about 1,000 km north to Baker Lake in Nunavut.
It lies close to the tree line, where the northern forest breaks up into open tundra.

q.q: Which river begins at Kasba Lake?

Q1699973.t: Two round lakes, two asteroids, 175 million years apart
Q1699973.s: Two almost perfectly round lakes lie side by side here, and both fill meteorite craters. The western one, about 36 km across, holds a striking ring of islands left by the impact. For decades the pair was taken for twins made by one double asteroid, but newer dating shows the eastern crater is roughly 175 million years older. In English they are the Clearwater Lakes.
Q1699973.w: Two round lakes side by side in the northern forest, the larger western one with a neat ring of islands inside it.
f: The western crater formed about 286 million years ago, the eastern one about 460–470 million years ago.
The western lake is about 36 km across, the eastern about 26 km.
The lakes lie in northern Quebec, roughly 100 km inland from the east coast of Hudson Bay.

q.q: What made the two round Clearwater Lakes?

Q1356838.t: The fur traders' shortcut from Montreal to the west
Q1356838.s: For two centuries of canoe travel, this lake was the hinge of the route west: paddlers came up the Ottawa and Mattawa rivers from Montreal, carried their canoes over a low height of land, then crossed Lake Nipissing and ran down the French River to Georgian Bay. Samuel de Champlain came this way in 1615. Today North Bay spreads along its north-eastern shore.
Q1356838.w: A wide, shallow lake with a scalloped shore and several large islands, with the city of North Bay on its north-eastern corner.
f: Although it covers about 870 km², the lake averages only around 4.5 m deep.
Its water flows west down the French River into Georgian Bay, part of Lake Huron.
Champlain crossed it in 1615 on his way to the country of the Huron-Wendat.

q.q: Which river carries Lake Nipissing's water to Georgian Bay?

Q1799611.t: A northern lake turned into a channel for diverted rivers
Q1799611.s: East of James Bay the taiga is a patchwork of lakes, bogs and black spruce, and Lake Sakami is one of its bigger pieces. It has also become part of an engineered water route: rivers farther south are diverted northward, and their water passes through Sakami on its way to the Robert-Bourassa Reservoir and the turbines of the La Grande River. A weir at its outlet keeps the lake from rising too high.
Q1799611.w: An irregular lake in flat, lake-strewn taiga, just south of the vast Robert-Bourassa Reservoir, about 140 km east of James Bay.
f: Water diverted from the Eastmain and Opinaca rivers flows through Sakami towards the La Grande power stations.
A canal with a concrete weir at the outlet limits how high the lake can rise.
The land around it is part of Eeyou Istchee, the Cree territory of James Bay.

q.q: Which reservoir receives the water flowing through Lake Sakami?

Q7359166.t: A lake cut in two by the 60th parallel
Q7359166.s: The ruler-straight line that divides Saskatchewan from the Northwest Territories, the 60th parallel, runs right through Scott Lake, so its water lies in two jurisdictions at once. On the ground nothing marks the border: only rocky shores, islands and dark spruce. The nearest community, Stony Rapids, is about 80 km to the south-east, and the lake's fishing lodge is reached by air.
Q7359166.w: A branching lake of rocky shores and islands in forest, lying on the 60° N line north-west of Stony Rapids.
f: The 60th parallel forms the whole northern border of Saskatchewan, about 445 km long.
At this latitude the midsummer sun stays up for nearly 19 hours.
Like most lakes here, it fills a hollow scraped into the Canadian Shield by Ice Age glaciers.

q.q: Which line runs through Scott Lake?

Q923693.t: A mountain lake inside a supervolcano
Q923693.s: At 2,357 m above sea level, Yellowstone Lake is the largest lake in North America at such a height — and it rests inside the caldera of one of the world's great volcanic systems. Its western bay, West Thumb, is itself a smaller caldera, and hot springs vent from the lake floor. Ice usually seals the surface from December until late May or June.
Q923693.w: A big lake shaped like an open hand, ringed by dark forest in the middle of the Yellowstone plateau.
f: Even from 11,000 m you are only about 8.6 km above its surface.
West Thumb formed in a volcanic eruption roughly 170,000 years ago.
Hot springs and steam vents on the lake bottom warm the water in places.

q.q: What is West Thumb, the western bay of Yellowstone Lake?

Q3518981.t: The giant among Arctic Alaska's thaw lakes
Q3518981.s: Alaska's North Slope is freckled with thousands of oval lakes, many lined up in the same direction by the prevailing wind. Teshekpuk is the giant among them: some 800 km² of shallow water barely above sea level, close to the Beaufort Sea. In summer tens of thousands of geese gather here to moult, and a caribou herd named after the lake calves on the tundra around it.
Q3518981.w: A huge, pale lake among countless smaller oval ponds on flat tundra, a short way inland from the Arctic Ocean coast.
f: It is the largest lake on Alaska's Arctic coastal plain, about 130 km south-east of Utqiaġvik.
Most lakes around it are thermokarst lakes, formed where permafrost thawed and the ground sank.
The Teshekpuk caribou herd takes its name from the lake.

q.q: What formed most of the lakes around Teshekpuk?

Q1427364.t: The biggest natural freshwater lake in the western US
Q1427364.s: Glaciers carved this basin at the foot of the Rockies, and Flathead Lake now fills it, roughly 45 km long. By surface area it is the largest natural freshwater lake west of the Mississippi in the lower 48 states. Sweet-cherry orchards line its eastern shore, and Wild Horse Island, near the west side, is a state park where bighorn sheep and a few wild horses roam.
Q1427364.w: A large blue lake at the head of a broad valley, with steep, often snowy mountains along its eastern side.
f: The southern half of the lake lies within the Flathead Indian Reservation.
A dam at the southern outlet near Polson controls the top few metres of the lake's level.
The peaks of Glacier National Park rise to the north-east.

q.q: Which animals share Wild Horse Island with a few wild horses?

Q1534419.t: Alberta's biggest lake, lost in a vast delta
Q1534419.s: Lake Claire is the largest lake lying entirely inside Alberta, yet it is very shallow — a broad sheet of water spread across the Peace–Athabasca Delta, one of the largest inland deltas in the world. Around it stretch sedge meadows, winding channels and willow flats inside Wood Buffalo National Park, where herds of free-roaming wood bison still graze.
Q1534419.w: A broad, shallow lake just west of Lake Athabasca, in a green-and-brown maze of delta channels and meadows.
f: Wood Buffalo is Canada's largest national park — bigger than Switzerland.
The Peace and Athabasca rivers feed the delta, and the lake rises and falls with their floods.
The park became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1983.

q.q: Which national park surrounds Lake Claire?

Q4539001.t: The smaller of Yamal's two 'sandy-shore' lakes
Q4539001.s: In the Nenets language 'to' means lake, and Yarroto is usually explained as 'lake with sandy shores'. There are two of them in southern Yamal; this one, the Second, covers about 154 km² but is no more than 8 m deep. For eight or nine months a year it is locked in ice, and in summer it glitters among thousands of smaller tundra lakes.
Q4539001.w: A large rounded lake with pale margins among countless smaller lakes, north-west of its bigger twin, Yarroto First.
f: The lake is about 21 km long and 8 km wide.
Nenets herders drive their reindeer across Yamal on long seasonal migrations.
Its fish include the peled, a whitefish common in Siberian lakes.

q.q: What does the Nenets word 'to' mean in names like Yarroto?

Q1520895.t: Western Siberia's biggest lake — and a shallow one
Q1520895.s: Lake Chany is the largest lake in Western Siberia, yet you could wade across much of it: the average depth is only about two metres. It has no outlet, so it swells and shrinks with wet and dry decades, and its water is slightly salty. From above it is a ragged patchwork of open water, reed beds and islands on the flat Baraba steppe.
Q1520895.w: A big, irregular sheet of grey-blue water with reedy bays and islands on flat steppe, about 350 km west of Novosibirsk.
f: Two rivers, the Kargat and the Chulym, flow into the lake, and none flows out.
The lake is made up of several linked basins, including Big Chany and Small Chany.
Its reed beds shelter huge numbers of ducks, grebes and gulls in summer.

q.q: How deep is Lake Chany on average?

Q537374.t: Where a river from Mongolia ends on the grasslands
Q537374.s: The Kherlen River rises in the mountains north-east of Ulaanbaatar, loops across Mongolia and finally ends here, in Hulun Lake, one of the largest lakes in China. Around it roll the treeless Hulunbuir grasslands, green in summer and brown and white in winter. When the ice is thick, fishermen still haul long nets out from under it in a famous winter catch.
Q537374.w: A large oval lake on open, treeless grassland, south of the border town of Manzhouli.
f: Its Russian name, Dalainor, comes from the Mongolian for 'sea lake'.
In wet years the lake spills through a channel into the Argun River, part of the Amur basin.
Its area changes with rainfall and has exceeded 2,000 km² in wet periods.

q.q: Which river flows from Mongolia into Hulun Lake?

Q673169.t: The lake 'where the water meets the sky'
Q673169.s: Bangweulu is said to mean 'where the water meets the sky', and on a hazy day it lives up to it: a flat, shining lake fading into endless swamps and floodplains. The wetlands shelter the shoebill, a huge grey bird with a clog-shaped bill, and the black lechwe, an antelope found nowhere else. David Livingstone died near its southern swamps in 1873.
Q673169.w: A flat, silvery lake that merges into vast green-brown swamps to the east and south.
f: Its water leaves by the Luapula River and ends up in the Congo, not the Nile.
Livingstone was still searching for the source of the Nile when he died at Chitambo's village.
In the rainy season the floodplains around the lake spread far beyond its open water.

q.q: Which great river system does Lake Bangweulu drain into?

Q203137.t: A Sámi lake of three thousand islands
Q203137.s: More than 3,000 islands are scattered across Lake Inari, so from the air it looks less like one lake than a shattered mirror dropped into the pine and birch forest of Lapland. It is Finland's third-largest lake and a heartland of Sámi culture; the rocky islet of Ukonsaari was once a sacred place of offerings. From about November to June the lake lies frozen under snow.
Q203137.w: A huge, shattered-looking lake crowded with islands in low northern forest, close to the Norwegian and Russian borders.
f: It covers about 1,040 km², making it the third-largest lake in Finland.
The lake drains north by the Paatsjoki River to the Barents Sea.
Inari lies roughly 270 km north of the Arctic Circle.

q.q: Roughly how many islands dot Lake Inari?

Q19253.t: An hourglass of a lake with a famous winter battle
Q19253.s: Two broad basins joined by a narrow waist give Lake Peipus the look of an hourglass, and the border between Estonia and Russia runs down its length. It is one of Europe's largest lakes, yet only about 7 m deep on average, so it freezes over most winters. In 1242 Alexander Nevsky's army defeated the Livonian knights on its ice, in what Russians call the Battle on the Ice.
Q19253.w: A huge hourglass-shaped lake — a wide northern basin, a narrow middle strait, a smaller southern basin — between Tartu and Pskov.
f: Its parts are Peipus proper in the north, narrow Lämmijärv ('Warm Lake') and Lake Pskov in the south.
The Narva River carries its water north to the Gulf of Finland.
Villages of Russian Old Believers have lined its western shore for centuries.

q.q: What does Lämmijärv, the narrow middle part of Lake Peipus, mean?

Q125912.t: A lovely lake with gas dissolved in its depths
Q125912.s: Lake Kivu looks idyllic from above: a long, deep-blue lake folded among steep green hills, with the big island of Idjwi in its middle. Its depths hide something rare — huge amounts of methane and carbon dioxide dissolved in the bottom water, held down by the weight of the lake. Today some of that methane is pumped up and burned to generate electricity on the Rwandan shore.
Q125912.w: A long, many-bayed blue lake among steep green hills, with a large island in the middle and volcanoes to the north.
f: The lake lies about 1,460 m above sea level and is nearly 500 m deep.
Idjwi, in the middle of the lake, is one of the largest lake islands in Africa.
Kivu drains south by the Ruzizi River into Lake Tanganyika.

q.q: Which gas is pumped from Lake Kivu's depths to make electricity?

Q125211.t: Hippos, a royal name and the Mountains of the Moon
Q125211.s: Just north of this lake the Rwenzori, the legendary Mountains of the Moon, sometimes show their glaciers above the clouds. Lake Edward itself lies on the floor of the Albertine Rift, shared by two national parks where hippos crowd the shallows. The explorer Henry Morton Stanley named it after the Prince of Wales, who later became King Edward VII.
Q125211.w: A broad blue lake on the floor of the rift valley, with a narrow channel running north-east to smaller Lake George.
f: The Kazinga Channel, about 32 km long, links it to Lake George and is famous for its hippos.
Its water leaves by the Semliki River, which flows to Lake Albert and on into the Nile.
The equator passes just north of the lake.

q.q: Which future king is Lake Edward named after?

Q140712.t: The lake behind China's strangest garden stones
Q140712.s: The holey, twisted limestone rocks that decorate Suzhou's classical gardens come from here: for centuries they were hauled out of Tai Hu and prized as 'Taihu stones'. The lake itself is broad and remarkably shallow, about two metres deep on average, and dotted with dozens of islands. Suzhou and Wuxi crowd its eastern and northern shores, a ring of lights at night.
Q140712.w: A huge, roughly round lake with islands and bays along its eastern side, west of Suzhou and the sprawl towards Shanghai.
f: At about 2,250 km², it is one of China's largest freshwater lakes.
The Grand Canal runs past its eastern side on the way between Suzhou and Hangzhou.
Biluochun, one of China's famous green teas, grows on the Dongting hills beside the lake.

q.q: What are 'Taihu stones' traditionally used for?

Q753898.t: Argentina's largest freshwater lake, tinted by glacier flour
Q753898.s: Glaciers grind the Andes into fine rock flour, and it tints Lago Argentino an unreal milky turquoise. This is the largest freshwater lake in Argentina, and its western arms reach deep into the ice: the Perito Moreno Glacier pushes right across one of them, now and then damming the water until it breaks through. The town of El Calafate sits on the southern shore, where mountains give way to dry steppe.
Q753898.w: A large turquoise lake with long fjord-like arms reaching west into snowy mountains and glaciers, and brown steppe to the east.
f: Its western arms lie within Los Glaciares National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1981.
The front of the Perito Moreno Glacier is about 5 km wide and rises some 60–70 m above the water.
The Upsala Glacier flows into the lake's long northern arm.

q.q: What gives Lago Argentino its milky turquoise colour?

Q651294.t: Tibet's 'Heavenly Lake', 4.7 km above the sea
Q651294.s: Namtso means 'heavenly lake' in Tibetan, and at about 4,718 m it sits closer to a cruising airliner than to the sea: the gap is only some 6 km. It is one of the largest lakes on the Tibetan Plateau, salty and startlingly blue, and one of Tibet's three holy lakes. To the south-east the snowy Nyenchen Tanglha range rises above 7,000 m.
Q651294.w: A large, intensely blue lake on a brown plateau, with a line of glaciated peaks along its south-eastern side.
f: Pilgrims walk around the lake; a circuit in the Tibetan Year of the Sheep is thought especially auspicious.
Nyenchen Tanglha, the highest peak of the range beside it, reaches 7,162 m.
In winter the whole lake freezes over.

q.q: What does the Tibetan name Namtso mean?

Q1774501.t: A Kolyma tundra lake named after the seal
Q1774501.s: Nerpichye means 'seal lake', a hint of how close the Arctic Ocean is: the lake lies in the Kolyma Lowland, on the left side of the Kolyma River's delta. It formed where permafrost thawed and the ground slumped, and its low, boggy shores barely rise above the water. Around it thousands of smaller lakes make the tundra look like lace.
Q1774501.w: A large lake stretched from south-east to north-west in flat tundra riddled with lakes, just west of the Kolyma delta.
f: The lake covers about 237 km² and is one of the largest in Yakutia's Nizhnekolymsky district.
Its only outflow, a channel called the Nerpichya Viska, leads to the neighbouring lake Maloye Pokhodskoye.
Ice covers it for most of the year in this far north-eastern corner of Yakutia.

q.q: What kind of lake is Nerpichye by origin?

Q4538999.t: The bigger twin: 247 km² of shallow tundra water
Q4538999.s: Yarroto First is the larger of a pair of lakes in southern Yamal: some 247 km² of water, 22 km long, yet nowhere deeper than about 8 m. Like its twin a little to the north-west, it carries a Nenets name read as 'lake with sandy shores'. In June the sun here does not set at all, and around then the ice finally breaks up.
Q4538999.w: A big oval lake with pale edges on flat tundra dotted with thousands of ponds, south-east of its smaller twin.
f: It is about 22 km long, and its greatest depth is only about 8 m.
It is one of the largest lakes on the Yamal Peninsula.
The lake lies about 150 km north of the Arctic Circle.

q.q: Roughly how deep is Yarroto First at its deepest?

ne-lk-1159113765.t: Surprisingly deep lakes in the heart of Yamal
ne-lk-1159113765.s: Most tundra lakes are only a few metres deep, but the Neyto lakes in the middle of Yamal break the rule: the deepest of them goes down more than 50 m. Together the group covers about 364 km², and its waters drain two ways — towards the Gulf of Ob and towards the Kara Sea. Around them lies flat, treeless tundra.
ne-lk-1159113765.w: A group of large, linked lakes in flat treeless tundra in the middle of the Yamal Peninsula.
f: The group's three main lakes are Neyto First, Yorto and Malto.
The deepest lake of the group reaches about 53 m.
In midwinter the sun does not rise here for more than a month.

q.q: How deep is the deepest of the Neyto lakes?

ne-lk-1159113781.t: Where the Mordyyakha starts its run to the Kara Sea
ne-lk-1159113781.s: Yambuto is the source of the Mordyyakha, one of the main rivers of central Yamal, which winds north-west to the Kara Sea. The lake spreads over roughly 119 km² of flat tundra, where permafrost lies just beneath the moss and summer lasts barely two months. In June and July the sun circles the sky without setting, and the water shines like foil.
ne-lk-1159113781.w: A large lake with a ragged outline in flat tundra, just east of the Neyto lakes in central Yamal.
f: The Mordyyakha flows out of Yambuto and reaches the Kara Sea at Sharapov Shar Bay.
Permafrost under central Yamal can reach down hundreds of metres.

q.q: Which river flows out of Lake Yambuto?

Q1315765.t: A forest lake drafted into a canal to the White Sea
Q1315765.s: Since 1933 ships travelling between the Baltic and the White Sea have crossed Vygozero: the White Sea–Baltic Canal uses the lake as part of its route, and dams raised its level to make it deep enough. The result is a sprawling, island-strewn expanse in the Karelian forest. From its northern end the Vyg River runs on to meet the White Sea at Belomorsk.
Q1315765.w: A large, ragged lake full of islands in Karelian forest, with the town of Segezha near its western shore.
f: Raising the water for the canal made the lake much larger than it had been.
The Segezha River brings in water from Segozero, which lies to the west.
The lake is frozen for about half the year.

q.q: Which canal runs through Vygozero?

Q1416209.t: One of Karelia's deepest lakes, raised by a dam
Q1416209.s: In its northern part Segozero plunges to more than 100 m, remarkably deep for a lake hidden in the Karelian forest. In 1957 a dam at the source of the Segezha River lifted the water by about six metres and turned the lake into a reservoir. More than 70 islands are scattered across it, while its south-western bays are shallow, rarely deeper than ten metres.
Q1416209.w: A large, irregular lake with scattered islands in dense forest, west of the even bigger Vygozero.
f: The 1957 dam raised the lake by about 6.3 m.
Its water flows out by the Segezha River into Vygozero.
The deepest water, more than 100 m down, lies in the north of the lake.

q.q: What happened to Segozero in 1957?
x: A canal linked it to the Volga

Q845891.s: From the bare hilltops of Koli, on Pielinen's western shore, Finnish artists of the 1890s looked down on a view that became a national symbol: long wooded islands afloat on a vast pale lake. From a plane you can take in far more of it than they could. In hard winters an ice road crosses the lake from Koli to the far shore.
Q845891.w: A long, wide lake running north–south through forested hills, with a steep wooded ridge on its western shore.
f: Koli's highest top, Ukko-Koli, rises to 347 m, about 250 m above the lake.
Pielinen drains south by the Pielisjoki River, through Joensuu, towards Lake Saimaa.
It covers about 894 km², making it one of Finland's largest lakes.

q.q: Which famous viewpoint rises on Pielinen's western shore?

Q709323.s: Topozero runs for some 75 km through the forests of northern Karelia, a long sheet of water strewn with 144 islands. It is the fourth-largest lake in the republic and deep for this region, reaching 56 m. Its water spills north by the Sofyanga River into Pyaozero, and since the 1960s both lakes have been part of the same hydropower reservoir.
Q709323.w: A long, broad lake with many islands in dense forest, south of Pyaozero and not far below the Arctic Circle.
f: The lake's open water covers about 986 km², and its islands add some 63 km² more.
Its average depth is around 16 m, and the deepest point is about 56 m.
It is about 75 km long and up to 30 km wide.

q.q: How many islands does Topozero have?

Q611206.t: A freshwater lake at the edge of the Tarim desert
Q611206.s: Snowmelt from the Tian Shan gathers in the Kaidu River and pools here, in Bosten Lake — the largest freshwater lake in Xinjiang, set among dry mountains and desert. Its outflow, the Peacock River, cuts through a gorge to water the oasis city of Korla. Wide reed beds fringe its shores, turning gold in autumn against the blue water.
Q611206.w: A large blue lake with reedy margins in a brown basin, south of the Tian Shan and north of the Taklamakan.
f: The lake covers roughly 1,000 km² and lies about 1,050 m above sea level.
The Kaidu River brings in most of its water, fed by Tian Shan snow and glaciers.
Korla, downstream on the Peacock River, is famous for its fragrant pears.

q.q: Which river flows out of Bosten Lake towards Korla?

Q207690.t: China's largest freshwater lake — for half the year
Q207690.s: In the summer floods Poyang is China's largest freshwater lake, a brown-green sea thousands of square kilometres wide. In the dry winter it shrinks back into channels and pools, exposing vast grassy flats. That is when the Siberian cranes arrive: nearly the entire world population of these white birds spends the winter here. Mount Lu rises above the north-western shore.
Q207690.w: A huge branching lake, or in winter a maze of channels and green flats, south of the Yangtze with Mount Lu to the north-west.
f: In some dry winters the lake shrinks to a small fraction of its summer size.
It meets the Yangtze at Hukou, whose name means 'lake mouth'.
Five main rivers of Jiangxi, the Gan among them, flow into it.

q.q: Nearly the world's entire population of which bird winters at Poyang?

ne-lk-1159114031.t: One of a chain of lakes on the Yangtze's north bank
ne-lk-1159114031.s: North of the Yangtze, just downstream of where Poyang Lake empties into it, a chain of shallow lakes spreads across the floodplain: Longgan, Huang, Daguan and Bo. Together they form one of the largest lake groups along the river's middle and lower course. Daguan's level rises with the summer floods and drops in winter, when migrating waterbirds gather on its shores.
ne-lk-1159114031.w: A shallow lake with a ragged outline among fields and other lakes, north of the Yangtze and north-east of Poyang Lake's outlet.
f: Daguan lies in Anhui province, in Susong and Wangjiang counties.
Neighbouring Longgan Lake is a national nature reserve for wintering waterbirds.

q.q: Which great river flows just south of Daguan Lake?

Q6673852.t: A lake shared by two provinces, busy with winter birds
Q6673852.s: Longgan Lake straddles the border of Hubei and Anhui provinces on the north side of the Yangtze, the westernmost of a chain of floodplain lakes. At high water it covers some 420 km², a shallow sheet among rice fields and fish ponds. Its Hubei part is a national nature reserve, where big flocks of ducks, geese and other waterbirds spend the winter.
Q6673852.w: A broad, shallow lake in flat farmland just north of the Yangtze, a short way north of the river's junction with Poyang Lake.
f: The lake lies partly in Huangmei County, Hubei, and partly in Susong County, Anhui.
The Hubei part is protected as a national nature reserve for wetland birds.
About 180 bird species, most of them waterbirds, have been recorded in the reserve.

q.q: Which two provinces share Longgan Lake?

Q7374197.t: Mother lake of Wuhan's most famous fish
Q7374197.s: Wuhan's best-known dish, Wuchang fish, is a bream that scientists first described from specimens caught here, and locals call Liangzi its 'mother lake'. The fish's fame spread across China after Mao Zedong mentioned it in a poem in 1956. From above, Liangzi is a many-armed lake with countless bays and islands, spread through green countryside south-east of Wuhan's sprawl.
Q7374197.w: A many-armed lake with dozens of bays and islands in green farmland south of the Yangtze, between Wuhan and Ezhou.
f: The type specimen of the blunt-snout bream, sold as Wuchang fish, came from Liangzi Lake.
Mao's 1956 line 'and now I eat Wuchang fish' made the dish famous across China.
It is one of the largest lakes of Hubei, long nicknamed the 'province of a thousand lakes'.

q.q: Which fish, famous in Wuhan cooking, was first described from Liangzi Lake?

Q1404973.t: The Tibetan lake that grew past Namtso
Q1404973.s: For a long time Namtso was the largest lake in Tibet, but Siling Co has overtaken it: fed by melting glaciers and heavier rain, it has swollen by hundreds of square kilometres in recent decades. It lies at about 4,530 m in a wide, empty basin of the Changtang plateau. The salty water is an intense blue, and black-necked cranes breed on the marshes around it.
Q1404973.w: A large, deep-blue lake with a lobed outline on a bare brown plateau, north-west of Namtso.
f: Its area grew from roughly 1,600 km² in the 1970s to more than 2,300 km² in recent years.
The lake lies at the heart of a reserve for the black-necked crane, the only crane of high plateaus.
Even at 4,530 m, the lake is still some 6.5 km lower than a cruising airliner.

q.q: Which lake did Siling Co overtake as Tibet's largest?

Q1323267.t: Mongolia's second-largest freshwater lake, in a dry basin
Q1323267.s: The Khovd River comes down from the Altai and spreads into a vast marshy delta before it reaches Khar-Us Nuur, Mongolia's second-largest freshwater lake. Reed beds, channels and a big island called Agbash fill much of it, so from above it looks more like a green-and-blue mosaic than open water. All around lies the dry, brown Great Lakes Depression of western Mongolia.
Q1323267.w: A large lake broken up by reeds and one big island, with a wide green delta on its western side, east of Khovd city.
f: Agbash Island, inside the lake, covers about 274 km².
A channel carries water from Khar-Us Nuur on to neighbouring Khar Nuur.
The lake and its delta are protected as a national park and a Ramsar wetland.

q.q: Which river forms the big delta at Khar-Us Nuur?

Q6403.t: A blue crescent with Mont Blanc on the horizon
Q6403.s: From cruise height Lake Geneva is an unmistakable blue crescent some 73 km long, with Geneva at one tip and the Rhône valley at the other. The northern shore is Swiss, most of the southern shore French. The Rhône flows in grey with glacier silt at the eastern end and leaves clear at Geneva. On a clear day Mont Blanc's white dome shines to the south-east.
Q6403.w: A large crescent-shaped lake curving between the Jura and the Alps, with Geneva at its south-western tip.
f: The lake is about 310 m deep at its deepest and covers around 580 km².
The terraced Lavaux vineyards on its northern shore are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Its French name, Lac Léman, comes from the Latin Lacus Lemannus.

q.q: Which river flows through Lake Geneva?

Q206942.t: The British Isles' biggest lake — a giant's handiwork?
Q206942.s: Legend says the giant Fionn mac Cumhaill scooped up a huge clod of earth and hurled it at a rival, leaving the hollow that filled to become Lough Neagh; the clod, they say, landed in the sea as the Isle of Man. The real origin is geological, but the lake is truly big — the largest in the British Isles by area. Belfast International Airport sits close to its eastern shore.
Q206942.w: A broad, roughly square lake in green farmland west of Belfast, with Belfast International Airport near its eastern shore.
f: Five of Northern Ireland's six counties touch its shores.
It supports one of Europe's largest commercial fisheries for wild eels.
Although it covers about 390 km², it averages only around 9 m deep.

q.q: How many of Northern Ireland's six counties touch Lough Neagh?

Q188195.t: Sweden's long, clear, cold blade of water
Q188195.s: Vättern is a slim blue blade about 135 km long, cutting north–south through southern Sweden. Its water is so clean and cold that it supplies drinking water to about a quarter of a million people. Jönköping curls around the southern tip, the long island of Visingsö floats in its southern half, and the Göta Canal crosses it on the way between the Baltic and Lake Vänern.
Q188195.w: A long, narrow lake running north–south, with Jönköping at its southern tip and a slim island in its southern half.
f: Vättern is Sweden's second-largest lake and reaches about 128 m deep.
The Göta Canal crosses the lake, linking the Baltic coast with Lake Vänern.
Vadstena, on the eastern shore, grew up around the abbey founded by St Birgitta's order in the 14th century.

q.q: Which canal crosses Lake Vättern?

Q845868.t: A big lake at 74° north, free of ice for only weeks
Q845868.s: At about 74° N, Lake Taymyr is one of the most northerly large lakes on Earth, and its ice usually breaks up only in July. It is vast but shallow, on average just a few metres deep, and its long arms reach towards the bare ridges of the Byrranga Mountains to the north. Musk oxen, brought back to Taymyr in the 1970s, graze the tundra around it.
Q845868.w: A long, many-armed lake on flat tundra, with the low, bare Byrranga Mountains rising to the north.
f: The Upper Taymyra River flows in, and the Lower Taymyra carries the water north to the Kara Sea.
Musk oxen were reintroduced to the Taymyr Peninsula from Canada and Alaska in 1974–1975.
Its area runs to thousands of square kilometres, yet its average depth is only about 3 m.

q.q: Which animals were brought back to Taymyr's tundra in the 1970s?

Q240398.t: A lake of 580 islands that doubled in size
Q240398.s: More than 580 islands are scattered across Kovdozero, so from above it reads like a jigsaw of dark forest pieces floating on grey-blue water. In 1955 a hydropower dam downstream raised its level by more than six metres, and the lake's surface roughly doubled. Its water runs on by the Kovda River to the White Sea's Kandalaksha Gulf, only a short distance to the east.
Q240398.w: A sprawling lake crowded with hundreds of wooded islands, just north of the Arctic Circle and west of the White Sea's Kandalaksha Gulf.
f: Before the dam the lake covered about 294 km²; its surface is now about 608 km².
Its islands, more than 580 of them, add up to some 70 km².
The Kovda cascade of power stations uses the lake's water on its short run to the sea.

q.q: What happened to Kovdozero's area after the 1955 dam?

Q1345130.t: A maze of 451 islands near Finland's eastern edge
Q1345130.s: Some 451 islands are scattered across Koitere, a maze of wooded strips and open water deep in the forests of Ilomantsi, in North Karelia. The easternmost point of Finland — and of the European Union — lies not far to the east. The Koitajoki River flows out towards the Pielisjoki, although most of the lake's outflow is sent through a tunnel to a hydropower plant at Pamilo.
Q1345130.w: An island-choked lake in unbroken forest near Finland's eastern border, about 60 km north-east of Joensuu.
f: The lake covers about 164 km² and holds some 451 islands.
Finland's easternmost point, on the lake Virmajärvi, is in the same municipality of Ilomantsi.
A tunnel sends most of the outflow to the Pamilo power station, bypassing about 20 km of river.

q.q: Where is most of Koitere's outflow sent?
x: Into a canal to Lake Saimaa

Q7334058.t: The lake that broke through and dropped 9.5 metres
Q7334058.s: In 1859 workers were digging a canal to lower this lake and win new farmland; instead the water broke through the sandy ridge of Jaamankangas and carved its own outlet. Within about a month Höytiäinen fell some 9.5 m and lost roughly a third of its area. Even so, it still spreads over about 283 km² of North Karelia, just north of Joensuu.
Q7334058.w: A large lake in forest just north of Joensuu, separated from the Pyhäselkä basin to the south-west by a sandy ridge.
f: The water level fell about 9.5 m within a month in 1859.
The lake shrank by roughly a third, and the exposed bed became new land.
Today it drains south-west into Pyhäselkä through the channel the water cut.

q.q: What happened to Höytiäinen in 1859?

Q203462.t: The lake on the old road from the Varangians to the Greeks
Q203462.s: A thousand years ago, merchants rowing from the Baltic towards Byzantium crossed Lake Ilmen: the route from the Varangians to the Greeks ran up the Volkhov, across the lake and on up the Lovat. At its northern tip the Volkhov leaves for Lake Ladoga, passing Veliky Novgorod. The lake is shallow and restless, swelling hugely each spring with meltwater from some fifty rivers.
Q203462.w: A broad, shallow lake in flat, marshy country, with Veliky Novgorod just beyond its northern tip on the Volkhov River.
f: In the spring flood its area can nearly triple compared with the low-water season.
More than 50 rivers, including the Msta, Lovat and Shelon, flow in; only the Volkhov flows out.
In the Novgorod tale of Sadko, the minstrel's music charms a king who rises from Lake Ilmen.

q.q: Which river flows out of Lake Ilmen?

Q580019.t: The 'Sea of Kainuu' and its old tar route
Q580019.s: Locals call Oulujärvi the Sea of Kainuu, and on a windy day its steep grey waves earn the name. In the 19th century the lake was a highway for tar: boats loaded with barrels crossed it and shot the rapids of the Oulujoki down to Oulu, then one of the world's great tar ports. Sandy islands and beaches rim its open water.
Q580019.w: A wide, open lake in Finland's forested interior, with Kajaani near its south-eastern end and a long wooded island in the middle.
f: The lake covers roughly 900 km², one of the largest areas of open water in Finland.
Its water flows west by the Oulujoki River to the Gulf of Bothnia at Oulu.
Manamansalo, a long sandy island, lies in the middle of the lake.

q.q: What cargo did boats carry across Oulujärvi towards Oulu in the 1800s?

Q1888211.t: A lake raised 3 m to send a river another way
Q1888211.s: Southern Indian Lake was once simply a wide stretch of the Churchill River. In 1976 a dam at Missi Falls raised it by about 3 m, and now much of the Churchill's water leaves by a new channel on the lake's southern side, heading for the Rat and Burntwood rivers and the power stations of the Nelson. From above it is a huge lake of many broad basins in dense forest.
Q1888211.w: A huge lake of many broad basins and islands in dense northern forest, on the Churchill River in northern Manitoba.
f: The dam at Missi Falls, at the lake's natural outlet, holds the water about 3 m above its old level.
A channel at South Bay sends water into the Rat River and on to the Nelson River's hydro plants.
The diversion carries on average about 875 cubic metres of water a second.

q.q: Which river's water is diverted out of Southern Indian Lake?

Q1052532.t: Where the Saskatchewan River pauses before Lake Winnipeg
Q1052532.s: The Saskatchewan River, which drains the prairies all the way from the Rocky Mountains, spreads into Cedar Lake before its final drop at Grand Rapids into Lake Winnipeg. Since the 1960s a hydroelectric dam at Grand Rapids has held the lake higher than before, drowning low shoreline forest and marsh. It is one link in the chain of big lakes that dominates the map of Manitoba.
Q1052532.w: A broad, irregular lake in flat forest and marsh, just north of Lake Winnipegosis and west of the north basin of Lake Winnipeg.
f: The Saskatchewan River flows through the lake and leaves by Grand Rapids for Lake Winnipeg.
The Grand Rapids generating station, finished in the 1960s, turned Cedar Lake into a reservoir.
Some of the river's water begins in glaciers of the Canadian Rockies.

q.q: Which river flows through Cedar Lake on its way to Lake Winnipeg?

Q979922.t: A near-round lake that feeds the Saguenay fjord
Q979922.s: Lac Saint-Jean is almost round, about 1,000 km² of water in a flat, farmed lowland ringed by forested hills, an unmistakable shape from the air. It is the source of the Saguenay River, which leaves from the eastern side at Alma and runs down to its famous fjord. People from around here are nicknamed 'Bleuets', after the wild blueberries that grow in abundance.
Q979922.w: A large, almost circular lake in a flat lowland with forested hills all around, north of Quebec City.
f: Each summer swimmers race about 32 km across it in the Traversée internationale du lac Saint-Jean.
Its big tributaries include the Péribonka, Mistassini and Ashuapmushuan rivers.
The ouananiche, a landlocked salmon, is the lake's emblem fish.

q.q: Which river flows out of Lac Saint-Jean?

Q22617464.t: The sprawling reservoir of the James Bay hydro giant
Q22617464.s: The Robert-Bourassa dam flooded some 2,800 km² of taiga in the late 1970s, turning hills into a maze of islands and long drowned valleys. Its water drives the Robert-Bourassa power station, carved deep into the rock and one of the largest underground power plants in the world. The spillway, ten giant steps blasted down a hillside, is nicknamed the Giant's Staircase.
Q22617464.w: A vast, branching reservoir full of islands in flat taiga, stretching east from the lower dams of the La Grande River.
f: The reservoir covers a little more than the area of Luxembourg.
It is named after Robert Bourassa, the Quebec premier who launched the James Bay project in 1971.
The nearby town of Radisson was built in the 1970s for the project's workers.

q.q: What is the Robert-Bourassa spillway nicknamed?

Q2179011.t: The next giant step up the La Grande River
Q2179011.s: Upstream of the Robert-Bourassa Reservoir, the La Grande River widens again into this second great artificial lake, created when the La Grande-3 dam closed in the early 1980s. It covers about 2,400 km², a ragged tangle of drowned valleys and hilltop islands that is hard to tell from the natural lakes around it. It is one step in a staircase of reservoirs and power stations descending towards James Bay.
Q2179011.w: A huge ragged reservoir with countless islands in flat taiga, east of the Robert-Bourassa Reservoir along the La Grande River.
f: The La Grande River drops through a series of dams and power stations before it reaches James Bay.
The gravel Trans-Taiga Road runs east past the reservoir deep into the interior of Quebec.
The La Grande complex is one of the largest hydroelectric systems in the world.

q.q: Into which bay does the La Grande River flow?

Q654515.t: A desert reservoir with a pale 'bathtub ring'
Q654515.s: Lake Mead fills the canyons of the Colorado behind the Hoover Dam, and when full it is the largest reservoir in the United States by capacity. Years of drought have pulled the water far below that mark, leaving a pale band of minerals on the canyon walls — the famous 'bathtub ring' that frames the dark-blue water in the reddish desert.
Q654515.w: Deep-blue water branching through reddish desert canyons, with a pale rim along the shores, about 40 km east of Las Vegas.
f: The Hoover Dam, at the lake's south-western end, was completed in 1936.
Las Vegas draws most of its water from the lake.
The lake is named after Elwood Mead, head of the Bureau of Reclamation while the dam was built.

q.q: Which dam holds back Lake Mead?

Q667507.t: A blue maze drowned in red-rock canyons
Q667507.s: Lake Powell is a startling sight from the air: fingers of deep-blue water threading through red and orange sandstone, filling the side canyons of the Colorado for nearly 300 km. It formed behind Glen Canyon Dam, closed in 1963, and took seventeen years to fill. It is named after John Wesley Powell, who led the first known expedition by boat through these canyons in 1869.
Q667507.w: Deep-blue water snaking through red-rock desert in countless branching canyons, with the dam and the town of Page at its south-western end.
f: Its winding shoreline is longer than the whole Pacific coast of the contiguous United States.
Rainbow Bridge, one of the world's largest natural stone arches, stands in one of its side canyons.
The lake straddles the border between Utah and Arizona.

q.q: Which explorer is Lake Powell named after?

Q1539726.t: A labyrinth of flooded lakes behind a silenced waterfall
Q1539726.s: In the early 1970s dams and dykes on the Labrador plateau joined dozens of lakes into the Smallwood Reservoir, a labyrinth of water covering roughly 6,500 km². Its water now drives the underground Churchill Falls power station instead of pouring over Churchill Falls itself, a cascade of about 75 m that is now mostly a trickle. The reservoir is named after Joey Smallwood, Newfoundland's first premier as a Canadian province.
Q1539726.w: A vast tangle of lakes, channels and islands on the flat, forested Labrador plateau, far inland from the Atlantic coast.
f: The Churchill Falls power station, built deep underground, is one of the largest hydroelectric plants in the world.
The reservoir swallowed older lakes, among them Michikamau and Lobstick.
Joey Smallwood led Newfoundland into Canada in 1949 and became its first premier.

q.q: What happened to Churchill Falls once the reservoir was built?
q.a: Most of its water was diverted

Q770141.t: A lake on the Niger that drowned Mungo Park's rapids
Q770141.s: The Scottish explorer Mungo Park died in 1806 in the rapids of the Niger at Bussa, while trying to follow the river to its mouth. Those rapids, and the old town of Bussa, now lie beneath Kainji Reservoir, formed when the Kainji Dam closed in the late 1960s. From above it is a long, many-armed lake in dry savanna, fed by the Niger from the north.
Q770141.w: A long, branching lake on the Niger River, running north–south through dry brown savanna in western Nigeria.
f: The Kainji Dam was completed in 1968, and a new town, New Bussa, replaced the drowned one.
Kainji Lake National Park stretches beside the reservoir.
When full, the reservoir covers about 1,200 km².

q.q: Which explorer died in rapids now drowned by Kainji Reservoir?

Q1540436.t: A former reservoir where a lost river meadow returns
Q1540436.s: For almost seventy years this stretch of the Dnipro was the 'Kakhovka Sea', a reservoir more than 200 km long. Since 2023 it has largely emptied, and the Dnipro once again winds through the old bed, where young willows and poplars have sprung up with astonishing speed. The floodplain drowned in the 1950s was the Great Meadow, a legendary haunt of the Zaporozhian Cossacks.
Q1540436.w: A long, wide valley of the Dnipro where the reservoir used to be: a green band of young forest with the river winding through it.
f: The reservoir was created in the 1950s by a dam at Nova Kakhovka.
When full, it covered about 2,150 km², one of the largest reservoirs on the Dnipro.
The Great Meadow was a vast floodplain of channels, woods and islands below the Dnipro rapids.

q.q: What was the floodplain under the Kakhovka Reservoir called?

Q1431500.t: The widest stretch of the Dnipro, an inland 'sea'
Q1431500.s: Here the Dnipro spreads so wide that people call it the Kremenchuk Sea: the reservoir is almost 30 km across in places and roughly 150 km long, the largest by area on the whole river. It filled in the early 1960s behind a dam near Kremenchuk. Cherkasy lines its western shore, where a long causeway and bridge carry road and rail across the water.
Q1431500.w: A very wide blue stretch of the Dnipro with flat farmland all round, and the city of Cherkasy along its western shore.
f: With about 2,250 km² of water, it is the largest reservoir on the Dnipro by area.
The Sula River enters from the east through wide marshes and reed beds.

q.q: Which river does the Kremenchuk Reservoir lie on?

Q745937.t: Europe's largest reservoir, where the Volga meets the Kama
Q745937.s: No reservoir in Europe covers more water. Behind the Zhiguli dam near Tolyatti the Volga backs up for some 500 km, and the Kama joins it in a vast bay south of Kazan. The reservoir filled in the late 1950s, drowning old riverside towns; Stavropol was moved and grew into Tolyatti. Near Ulyanovsk the water spreads so wide that the bridges across it run for kilometres.
Q745937.w: A huge, branching expanse of the Volga, many kilometres wide, with the city of Ulyanovsk on its western bank.
f: With about 6,450 km² of water, it is the largest reservoir in Europe.
Sviyazhsk, an old town near Kazan, became an island when the reservoir filled in 1957.
The ruins of Bolgar, capital of Volga Bulgaria, stand on its eastern shore and are a UNESCO site.

q.q: Which river joins the Volga inside the Kuybyshev Reservoir?

Q3234165.t: Where the backlands really did turn into sea
Q3234165.s: 'The backlands will become sea,' goes an old prophecy of the Brazilian sertão, and at Sobradinho it came true. In the late 1970s a dam on the São Francisco River flooded more than 4,000 km² of dry scrubland, creating one of the largest artificial lakes in the world by area. Several riverside towns had to be rebuilt on higher ground.
Q3234165.w: A huge, long lake of blue-grey water stretching through dry scrubland along the São Francisco River in northern Bahia.
f: The São Francisco is the longest river that flows entirely within Brazil.
Towns including Remanso, Casa Nova, Sento Sé and Pilão Arcado were rebuilt away from the rising water.
The reservoir also evens out the river's flow for the power stations farther downstream.

q.q: Which river is dammed to form the Sobradinho Reservoir?

Q1464758.t: The Caribbean's lowest point — with crocodiles
Q1464758.s: Lago Enriquillo lies well below sea level, the lowest point in the Caribbean, in a hot, dry trough between two mountain ranges. Its water is saltier than the ocean, yet American crocodiles live here, and rhinoceros iguanas roam Isla Cabritos in the middle. The lake takes its name from Enriquillo, a Taíno chief who held out against the Spanish in the nearby mountains.
Q1464758.w: A long, pale-blue lake with a large island, in a hot dry valley between mountain ranges in the south-west of the Dominican Republic.
f: No point in the Caribbean islands lies lower than the surface of this lake.
Isla Cabritos, in the middle of the lake, is a national park known for its iguanas.
Since the early 2000s the lake has risen markedly, drowning roads and farmland.

q.q: Which reptile lives in salty Lago Enriquillo?

Q199551.t: A great salt lake turned red and white
Q199551.s: Lake Urmia was once one of the largest salt lakes in the world, a long turquoise sheet in north-western Iran. In recent decades it has lost most of its water, and much of its bed is now a glaring white salt flat. What remains can turn blood-red in summer, when salt-loving algae and bacteria bloom. A long causeway still runs straight across the middle.
Q199551.w: A long basin of white salt flats and patches of red or turquoise water, with a straight causeway crossing its middle.
f: Its water became so salty that little but brine shrimp and microbes can live in it.
Flamingos have long bred on its islands in years with enough water.
The lake has no outlet; water leaves only by evaporation.

q.q: What turns Lake Urmia's water red in some summers?

Q257416.t: A desert lake filled by water drained from fields
Q257416.s: Before the 1960s this was largely a dry, salty hollow in the Karakum desert; today it holds one of the largest lakes in Central Asia. The water comes from farming: salty runoff from the irrigated cotton and rice fields of the lower Amu Darya is carried here by drainage canals. Long ago the river itself sometimes turned this way, and its water flowed on towards the Caspian.
Q257416.w: A large, irregular turquoise lake in brown desert, south of the pale cliffs of the Ustyurt plateau.
f: The lake fills a depression whose floor lies below sea level.
Nothing flows out, so its water grows steadily saltier.
The Uzboy, a dry ancient riverbed, once carried water from here towards the Caspian Sea.

q.q: Where does most of Sarygamysh Lake's water come from?

Q310547.t: A 'motley lake' at the mouth of a windy gate
Q310547.s: Alakol means 'motley lake', and its colours shift from turquoise to steel-grey as clouds race across it. They race for a reason: to the south-east lies the Dzungarian Gate, a mountain corridor between Kazakhstan and China through which fierce winds funnel. Holidaymakers prize its salty water, and islands in the lake shelter colonies of the rare relict gull.
Q310547.w: A large salt lake in a dry basin, with a narrow gap between mountains to its south-east leading towards China.
f: The Ebe, a cold wind that blasts through the Dzungarian Gate, can reach storm force.
The lake has no outlet, which is why its water is salty.
For thousands of years the Dzungarian Gate has been a route for nomads and traders.

q.q: What does the name Alakol mean?

Q21837060.t: South America's largest salt lake, pink with flamingos
Q21837060.s: Mar Chiquita means 'little sea', and in wet years this salt lake on the plains of Córdoba spreads over thousands of square kilometres, the largest in South America. Its size swings with the rains: in the 1970s and 80s it rose so fast that part of the resort town of Miramar was swallowed. Big flocks of flamingos feed in its shallows, turning stretches of shore pink.
Q21837060.w: A vast, pale, shallow lake on the flat pampas, often edged with white salt, north-east of the city of Córdoba.
f: Three species of flamingo feed on the lake.
Since 2022 the lake and its wetlands have been protected as Ansenuza National Park.
The Dulce River brings in much of its water from the north.

q.q: What does the Spanish name Mar Chiquita mean?

Q211823.t: Turkey's salt pan, white as snow in summer
Q211823.s: In summer most of Lake Tuz dries out into a dazzling white crust of salt, so bright it looks like snow lying in the middle of the Anatolian steppe. It is Turkey's second-largest lake, yet only a metre or two deep, and one of the saltiest lakes on Earth. Salt works along its shores produce much of the salt eaten in Turkey.
Q211823.w: A huge white or pale-blue patch on the brown Anatolian plateau, roughly midway between Ankara and Konya.
f: Its name simply means 'Salt Lake' in Turkish.
Greater flamingos gather on its islands to breed.
The lake lies about 905 m above sea level in a basin with no outlet.

q.q: What does 'Tuz' mean in Turkish?

Q126307.t: A soda sea on the Anatolian plateau, 1,640 m up
Q126307.s: Lake Van is so big and so alkaline that it feels like an inland sea: its water is rich in soda and feels soapy to the touch. The lake formed when lava from the Nemrut volcano blocked its outlet, and the snowy volcano Süphan, over 4,000 m high, still rises above the north shore. Only one fish, the pearl mullet, has adapted to its water.
Q126307.w: A huge blue lake on a high plateau, with a snowy volcano on its northern shore and a crater-topped mountain at its western end.
f: Van is Turkey's largest lake, covering about 3,700 km² at some 1,640 m above sea level.
Each spring pearl mullet swim up freshwater streams to spawn.
On Akdamar Island stands a 10th-century church famous for its stone carvings.

q.q: What blocked Lake Van's outlet and created the lake?

Q199903.t: A calm lake filling the crater of a super-eruption
Q199903.s: Lake Taupō, New Zealand's largest lake, fills a caldera left by some of the most violent eruptions of recent geological time. About 25,500 years ago the Oruanui eruption buried much of the North Island in ash and pumice, and around 1,800 years ago another eruption sent flows of hot pumice racing across the land. Today the calm blue water drains into the Waikato, New Zealand's longest river.
Q199903.w: A large, rounded blue lake in the middle of the North Island, with the snowy volcanoes of Tongariro rising to the south.
f: The lake covers about 616 km² and is up to about 186 m deep.
The Waikato River, New Zealand's longest, flows out at the town of Taupō.
Trout introduced in the 19th century draw anglers from around the world.

q.q: Which river flows out of Lake Taupō?

Q940488.t: The short river that carries all of Lake Superior
Q940488.s: Every drop of water leaving Lake Superior passes down the St. Marys River on its way to Lake Huron. At the twin cities of Sault Ste. Marie it tumbles about 6 m over rapids, which is why ships climb and descend through the Soo Locks beside them. Below the rapids the river braids around large islands and widens into lakes before reaching Huron.
Q940488.w: A broad river channel with big islands and lake-like widenings, running south-east from the twin cities of Sault Ste. Marie.
f: The river is about 120 km long and forms part of the border between the United States and Canada.
The Soo Locks let ships bypass the rapids, where Superior's level drops about 6 m to Huron's.
Sault Ste. Marie grew from a French mission founded in 1668, among the oldest in the Great Lakes region.

q.q: Which two lakes does the St. Marys River connect?

Q188203.t: A funnel of sea with one of the world's biggest tides
Q188203.s: Twice a day the sea surges up the Bristol Channel into the Severn Estuary, where the tide can rise and fall by around 14 m, one of the greatest tidal ranges in the world. The funnel shape does it: the channel narrows and shallows between the coasts of Wales and south-west England, squeezing the incoming water higher. Near its mouth the granite island of Lundy stands guard.
Q188203.w: A wide inlet narrowing eastward between the green coasts of south Wales and Devon, with a small island near its mouth.
f: Where the channel meets the Severn Estuary, the tidal range can reach about 14 m.
The rising tide pushes a wave called the Severn Bore far up the river.
Lundy's name comes from the Old Norse for 'puffin island'.

q.q: What does the name of Lundy island mean in Old Norse?

Q1971856.t: An island-studded sea where planes land on a beach
Q1971856.s: Between the long chain of the Outer Hebrides and the mountainous islands of Skye, Rùm, Coll and Tiree lies the Sea of the Hebrides, scattered with islands of every size. On Barra, at its western edge, scheduled flights land on the sands of Traigh Mhòr, and the timetable follows the tides. In summer basking sharks and minke whales feed in these cold, rich waters.
Q1971856.w: Grey-blue sea scattered with islands, between the long Outer Hebrides chain to the west and Skye's jagged mountains to the east.
f: Barra's airport uses a tidal beach as its runway, a rarity among scheduled airports.
The Cuillin ridge on Skye is one of the most rugged mountain ranges in Britain.
Basking sharks, the world's second-largest fish, are often seen here in summer.

q.q: What serves as the runway at Barra's airport?

Q35000.t: The world's shallowest sea, rimmed by pink lagoons
Q35000.s: No sea on Earth is shallower: the Sea of Azov is nowhere deeper than about 14 m, and much of it is far less. Two great rivers, the Don and the Kuban, pour in fresh water, so it is only mildly salty and often freezes in winter. On its western side the thin Arabat Spit, over 100 km long, walls off the Sivash, a maze of lagoons tinted pink and red.
Q35000.w: An enclosed greenish sea with a long, thread-thin sand spit along its western shore and pinkish lagoons behind it.
f: Its greatest depth is only about 14 m.
The narrow Kerch Strait connects it with the Black Sea.
The Sivash lagoons are so salty that microscopic algae tint them pink.

q.q: Roughly how deep is the Sea of Azov at its deepest?

Q14686.t: Two capitals and an imperial city on one Baltic gulf
Q14686.s: Helsinki and Tallinn face each other across the Gulf of Finland, only about 80 km apart, and at its far eastern end lies St Petersburg, Russia's capital for two centuries. The gulf is shallow and barely salty, so in cold winters its eastern part freezes over. Near St Petersburg a thin line crosses the water: a flood barrier running through Kotlin Island.
Q14686.w: A long, narrow arm of the Baltic running east, with Helsinki on the north shore, Tallinn on the south and St Petersburg at its head.
f: The Neva, entering at St Petersburg, carries more water than any other river flowing into the Baltic.
The St Petersburg flood barrier stretches about 25 km across the head of the gulf.
Thousands of rocky islands and skerries line the Finnish coast.

q.q: Which two capitals face each other across the Gulf of Finland?

Q210118.t: A curving coast of lagoons, flamingos and pink salt pans
Q210118.s: The Gulf of Lion sweeps in a broad arc from the Pyrenees to Provence, and its shore is a string of lagoons cut off from the sea by thin sandbars. In the middle sprawls the Camargue, the Rhône delta, where salt pans glow pink and flamingos wade. Two cold winds, the Mistral and the Tramontane, often rush down here, whipping the sea white.
Q210118.w: A wide, gently curved bay of the Mediterranean with a lagoon-lined coast, the Rhône delta in the middle and the Pyrenees at its south-western end.
f: The salt pans of Aigues-Mortes and Salin-de-Giraud turn pink thanks to salt-loving microalgae.
The Camargue is one of the main breeding grounds of greater flamingos in the Mediterranean.
The Canal du Midi ends in the Étang de Thau, the big lagoon beside the port of Sète.

q.q: Which river's delta forms the Camargue?

Q232912.t: Where the Gulf Stream races out into the Atlantic
Q232912.s: A river runs through this sea: the Florida Current, the start of the Gulf Stream, pours north through the strait carrying more water than all the world's rivers combined. From above, the deep channel shows dark indigo, sharply edged by the glowing turquoise shallows of the Bahama Banks to the east. Florida's coast and the curve of the Keys frame it to the west.
Q232912.w: Deep indigo water between the Florida coast and the brilliant turquoise shallows of the Bahama Banks.
f: At its core the current moves faster than a person walks.
Ponce de León's pilots noticed the powerful current here in 1513.
The strait separates the Florida Keys from Cuba, about 150 km to the south.

q.q: Which famous current flows through the Florida Strait?

Q140290.t: Named by Cook for the food it gave his crew
Q140290.s: When James Cook sailed along this coast in 1769, Māori communities supplied his ship generously, and he called it the Bay of Plenty. The name still fits: behind long white beaches spread kiwifruit and avocado orchards, and the town of Te Puke calls itself the kiwifruit capital of the world. The volcanic cone of Mauao stands guard at the entrance to Tauranga Harbour.
Q140290.w: A broad, open bay on the North Island's northern coast, with long beaches, a small cone at Tauranga harbour and islands offshore.
f: Cook named Poverty Bay, farther east, after a stop where he could get nothing he wanted.
Mayor Island (Tūhua), offshore, was an important source of obsidian for early Māori.
Mauao, at Tauranga's harbour entrance, is an extinct volcano about 230 m high.

q.q: Why did Cook name it the Bay of Plenty?

Q2565098.t: Open Pacific between Haida Gwaii and Vancouver Island
Q2565098.s: Between the southern tip of Haida Gwaii and the northern end of Vancouver Island, the coast of British Columbia opens straight onto the Pacific, and Queen Charlotte Sound takes the full force of its swells. Ships following the sheltered Inside Passage must cross this exposed stretch. To the east the mainland shatters into fjords and islands cloaked in the Great Bear Rainforest.
Q2565098.w: Open ocean between the north tip of Vancouver Island and Haida Gwaii, with a coast of fjords and forested islands to the east.
f: Haida Gwaii, to the north-west, was known as the Queen Charlotte Islands until 2010.
The Great Bear Rainforest on the mainland coast is one of the largest temperate rainforests in the world.
Humpback and grey whales pass along this coast on their long migrations.

q.q: What was Haida Gwaii called until 2010?

Q212428.t: A gulf of limestone towers and one tide a day
Q212428.s: In the north-western corner of the Gulf of Tonkin, some 1,600 limestone islands rise straight out of green water — Ha Long Bay, one of Asia's most famous seascapes. The gulf is shallow and sheltered by the big island of Hainan to the east. Its tides are unusual too: along much of this coast the sea rises and falls only once a day, not twice.
Q212428.w: A broad, shallow gulf between Vietnam's coast and the island of Hainan, with a maze of rocky islets in its north-western corner.
f: Ha Long Bay's limestone islands and islets are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
The Red River pours reddish-brown silt into the gulf's western side.
In Vietnamese it is called Vịnh Bắc Bộ, the Gulf of the North.

q.q: How many high tides a day does much of the Gulf of Tonkin get?

Q181857.t: The highest tides on Earth, twice a day
Q181857.s: Twice a day the Bay of Fundy fills and empties, and in its upper reaches the tide rises by as much as 16 m — the highest tides on Earth. At low water, vast red-brown mudflats appear where boats floated a few hours before. The long funnel of the bay does the work: its natural rhythm almost matches the ocean tide, so the water piles up higher and higher.
Q181857.w: A long, funnel-shaped bay between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, its upper arms edged with wide red-brown mudflats.
f: In the Minas Basin the difference between high and low tide can reach about 16 m.
At Hopewell Rocks, visitors walk on the sea floor at low tide around rocks shaped like giant flowerpots.
The Joggins Fossil Cliffs on its shore preserve forests from some 300 million years ago.

q.q: Roughly how high can the Bay of Fundy's tides reach?

Q35827.t: A brown 'river' so wide the far shore vanishes
Q35827.s: The Paraná and Uruguay rivers meet and pour into the Atlantic through the Río de la Plata, a funnel of brown, silty water up to about 220 km wide at its mouth. It is often called the widest river in the world, though geographers class it as an estuary. Buenos Aires spreads along one shore and Montevideo sits on the other, where brown river water meets the blue sea.
Q35827.w: A huge funnel of brown water opening to the south-east, with the sprawl of Buenos Aires on its south-western shore and Montevideo on the north.
f: Spanish explorers named it the 'River of Silver', hoping it led to silver mines inland.
Two capitals, Buenos Aires and Montevideo, face each other across it.
Its muddy colour comes from sediment carried down by the Paraná, one of South America's great rivers.

q.q: Which two rivers join to form the Río de la Plata?

Q205655.t: A strait so busy that ships dot it like grains of rice
Q205655.s: On a clear day the Singapore Strait looks peppered with white dots: tankers, container ships and bulk carriers under way or waiting at anchor, each trailing a thin wake. This narrow channel, only about 16 km wide, links the Strait of Malacca with the South China Sea and is one of the busiest shipping lanes on Earth. Singapore lies on the north side, Indonesia's Riau Islands on the south.
Q205655.w: A narrow channel crowded with ships, between the dense city of Singapore to the north and the green islands of Batam and Bintan.
f: The strait is about 105 km long.
The Port of Singapore is one of the busiest container ports in the world.
At night the anchored ships glitter like a floating city.

q.q: Which two waters does the Singapore Strait link?
q.a: Malacca Strait and South China Sea
x: Andaman Sea and Gulf of Thailand

Q52052.t: The sea gate between Korea and Japan, split by Tsushima
Q52052.s: Only about 200 km of water separate Korea from Japan's island of Kyushu here, and the island of Tsushima sits in the middle, splitting the strait into two channels. On a clear day Busan's coast and Tsushima's green hills can be seen at the same time from cruise height. A warm current from the south flows through, keeping the Japanese shores of the Sea of Japan milder.
Q52052.w: A broad strait between Korea's south coast and Kyushu, with the long, hilly island of Tsushima in the middle.
f: Tsushima lies only about 50 km from the Korean coast.
The warm Tsushima Current, a branch of the Kuroshio, flows north-east through the strait.
Ferries link Busan and Fukuoka across the strait in a matter of hours.

q.q: Which island divides the Korea Strait into two channels?

Q231312.t: A sea of three thousand islands stitched by bridges
Q231312.s: Some 3,000 islands are scattered across the Seto Inland Sea, the calm water enclosed by Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu. Three chains of bridges now stitch Honshu to Shikoku across it; from cruise height they show as fine threads hopping from island to island. At the Naruto Strait, on its eastern edge, the tide spins whirlpools up to about 20 m across.
Q231312.w: A long, calm inland sea crowded with green islands between Honshu and Shikoku, crossed by several chains of bridges.
f: The Akashi Kaikyō Bridge, at its eastern end, held the record for the longest suspension span from 1998 to 2022.
Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima, with its torii gate standing in the sea, is a UNESCO site.
In 1934 the Inland Sea became one of Japan's first national parks.

q.q: Which two main islands of Japan are linked by bridges across this sea?

Q127031.t: A shallow strait that was dry land in the Ice Age
Q127031.s: Between the mountainous island of Taiwan and the coast of Fujian lies a strait about 130 to 180 km wide, yet surprisingly shallow, mostly less than 100 m deep. During the last Ice Age, when sea level fell, much of it was dry land that animals could walk across. In the middle lie the low, flat Penghu Islands, fringed with pale reefs.
Q127031.w: A wide channel between the high, cloud-capped mountains of Taiwan and the Fujian coast, with a cluster of flat islands in the middle.
f: Its narrowest crossing is about 130 km.
The Penghu Islands are famous for cliffs of columnar basalt.
Fishing boats sometimes haul up fossils of Ice Age animals from its sea floor.

q.q: What was much of the Taiwan Strait during the last Ice Age?

Q1129590.t: A tidal inlet guarded by a row of volcanoes
Q1129590.s: Tikahtnu, the Dena'ina name for Cook Inlet, runs about 290 km from the Gulf of Alaska up to Anchorage, and its tides are among the biggest in North America. Along its western shore stands a line of volcanoes — Augustine, Iliamna, Redoubt and Spurr — often snow-capped and sometimes steaming. James Cook sailed in here in 1778, hoping it might lead to a passage to the Atlantic.
Q1129590.w: A long, silty-grey inlet running north-east towards Anchorage, with snowy volcanic cones along its western shore.
f: At Anchorage the tide can rise and fall by about 9 m.
Augustine volcano forms its own island near the inlet's mouth.
A small, isolated population of beluga whales lives in these waters.

q.q: Which city stands at the head of Cook Inlet?

Q917872.t: Home of the world's biggest sockeye salmon run
Q917872.s: Every summer tens of millions of sockeye salmon swim in from the Bering Sea and head up the rivers that drain into Bristol Bay — the largest run of these fish anywhere on Earth. Fishing boats crowd its muddy estuaries in July, and brown bears line the streams inland. James Cook named the bay in 1778 after Admiral the Earl of Bristol.
Q917872.w: A broad, shallow bay of the Bering Sea, with the long Alaska Peninsula forming its southern shore.
f: Male walruses haul out by the thousand on Round Island, in the north of the bay.
The Kvichak River carries water from Lake Iliamna, Alaska's largest lake, into the bay.
Katmai National Park, famous for bears fishing at Brooks Falls, lies on its south-eastern side.

q.q: Which fish makes Bristol Bay famous?

Q2336534.t: Where Greenland's ice sheet spills into the sea
Q2336534.s: Along Melville Bay the Greenland ice sheet reaches the sea almost without a break, pouring through dozens of glaciers that calve icebergs into the water. For 19th-century whalers this was one of the most feared stretches of the Arctic: many ships were crushed by drifting ice while trying to pass. Today much of it is a nature reserve, home to polar bears and narwhals.
Q2336534.w: A wide bay on Greenland's north-west coast where the white ice sheet spills straight into a sea full of icebergs.
f: The Melville Bay Nature Reserve protects polar bears and narwhals.
John Ross named it in 1818 after Viscount Melville, First Lord of the Admiralty.
Sea ice covers the bay for much of the year.

q.q: Which Arctic whale with a single long tusk lives in Melville Bay?

Q876470.t: A cold, whale-rich sea closed off by an undersea bank
Q876470.s: From the curled arm of Cape Cod to the tip of Nova Scotia, the Gulf of Maine is almost a sea of its own, cut off from the open Atlantic by the shallow Georges Bank. Its cold, rich water draws humpback and right whales to feed. Along the Maine coast, thousands of rocky islands and drowned valleys make one of the most ragged shorelines in America.
Q876470.w: A broad, cold gulf edged by the sandy hook of Cape Cod to the south-west and the rocky, island-studded coast of Maine to the north.
f: The Bay of Fundy, with the world's highest tides, is one of its arms.
Georges Bank, at its mouth, was for centuries one of the richest fishing grounds on Earth.
For part of the year, Cadillac Mountain on its coast is among the first places in the US to see sunrise.

q.q: Which shallow undersea bank partly encloses the Gulf of Maine?

Q216868.t: America's largest estuary, over an ancient impact crater
Q216868.s: Chesapeake Bay runs some 300 km from the mouth of the Susquehanna to the Atlantic, a branching estuary fed by dozens of rivers and the largest in the United States. Its mouth hides a surprise: an asteroid crater about 35 million years old, buried under sediment. There a thin bridge line crosses the water and twice seems to vanish — the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel diving underwater.
Q216868.w: A long, branching bay with many river mouths, running north–south from Maryland to Virginia's Atlantic coast.
f: The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel is about 28 km long, with two tunnels that let ships pass over them.
The bay is famous for its blue crabs.
More than 150 rivers and streams flow into it.

q.q: What lies buried beneath the mouth of Chesapeake Bay?

Q1536292.t: A Patagonian bay where water-seekers struck oil
Q1536292.s: In 1907 drillers at Comodoro Rivadavia, on the shore of this gulf, were searching for fresh water in the parched Patagonian steppe. They struck oil instead, and Argentina's oil industry was born. Today the San Jorge Gulf is a broad, windswept bay about 250 km across, its dry brown shores dotted with oil wells and scoured by strong westerly winds.
Q1536292.w: A wide, semicircular bay on the Patagonian coast, edged by dry brown tablelands, with Comodoro Rivadavia on its western shore.
f: The gulf stretches about 250 km between Cape Dos Bahías and Cape Tres Puntas.
The San Jorge basin around it is one of Argentina's main oil-producing regions.

q.q: What did drillers looking for water find at Comodoro Rivadavia in 1907?

Q200712.t: Turquoise shallows between Spain and its islands
Q200712.s: The Balearic Sea lies between Spain's Mediterranean coast and the islands of Mallorca, Ibiza and Formentera. Where it is shallow, meadows of Posidonia seagrass over pale sand make the water glow turquoise, especially in the channel between Ibiza and Formentera. On the mainland side the Ebro delta pushes a green-and-brown triangle far out into the blue.
Q200712.w: Deep-blue sea between the Spanish coast and the Balearic Islands, with turquoise shallows around Ibiza and the Ebro delta jutting from the mainland.
f: The Posidonia meadows between Ibiza and Formentera are part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Posidonia is not a seaweed but a flowering plant found only in the Mediterranean.
Much of the Ebro delta, one of the largest wetlands in the western Mediterranean, is covered with rice fields.

q.q: What makes the shallows around Ibiza and Formentera glow turquoise?

Q34575.t: A sea of islands with a drowned volcano at its heart
