Q34575.s: Thousands of islands are scattered across the Aegean between the coasts of Greece and Anatolia, and from cruise height they look like crumbs of brown and white on deep blue. In the south, a broken ring of cliffs around a flooded bay is Santorini, the rim of a volcano that erupted about 3,600 years ago. In summer the strong meltemi wind streaks the sea with whitecaps.
Q34575.w: Deep-blue sea scattered with rocky brown islands, with a broken ring-shaped island in the south.
f: In Greek myth it is named after King Aegeus, who threw himself into the sea believing his son Theseus was dead.
The Cyclades take their name from the circle they form around the sacred island of Delos.
The meltemi, a dry northerly wind, blows across it through much of the summer.

q.q: In Greek myth, which king gave his name to the Aegean Sea?

Q622811.t: A sea edged by a chain of sandbanks called Adam's Bridge
Q622811.s: Between India and Sri Lanka runs a strange line of shoals and sandbanks about 48 km long, pale against turquoise water: Adam's Bridge, known in India as Rama Setu, the bridge that the Ramayana says Rama's army built. It marks the northern edge of the Gulf of Mannar, a warm sea of coral islets, seagrass and dugongs. For centuries its oyster beds were famous for pearls.
Q622811.w: A string of pale sandbanks linking India's Pamban Island with Sri Lanka's Mannar Island, with turquoise shallows to the south.
f: Twenty-one small islands in the gulf make up India's Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park.
Dugongs, the sea cows that graze on seagrass, still live in the gulf.
The pearl fisheries off Thoothukudi (Tuticorin) have been known since ancient times.

q.q: What is the chain of shoals between India and Sri Lanka called?

Q181969.t: China's inner sea, where the Yellow River ends
Q181969.s: The Bohai is almost enclosed: the Liaodong and Shandong peninsulas reach towards each other and leave only a narrow, island-strewn gap to the Yellow Sea. It is shallow, averaging less than 20 m, and in hard winters ice forms along its shores. On the south-western side a brown plume fans into the sea — the mouth of the Yellow River, whose delta keeps growing.
Q181969.w: A nearly enclosed, often murky sea between two peninsulas, with a brown river plume on its south-western shore.
f: The Great Wall meets the sea at Shanhaiguan, on its north-western shore.
Tianjin, one of China's biggest ports, stands on its western shore.
The Bohai Strait between the two peninsulas is only about 100 km wide.

q.q: Which great river flows into the Bohai Sea?

Q844917.t: Coral reefs, mangroves and a salt desert next door
Q844917.s: The Gulf of Kutch pushes about 160 km into the coast of Gujarat, a funnel of muddy water with strong tides. Yet its southern shore hides coral reefs and mangrove islands, protected since 1982 as India's first marine national park. To the north stretches the Rann of Kutch, a vast salt marsh that turns into a dazzling white desert in the dry season.
Q844917.w: A long, funnel-shaped gulf of brownish water on India's west coast, with mangrove-fringed islands in the south and white salt flats to the north.
f: Tides in the inner gulf rise and fall by several metres, among the largest on India's coast.
Big cargo ports at Kandla and Mundra stand on its northern shore.
Dolphins, sea turtles and a few dugongs live in the marine national park.

q.q: What was set up in the Gulf of Kutch in 1982?

Q645012.t: Where ships queue for the Panama Canal
Q645012.s: At the head of the Gulf of Panama, dozens of ships often lie at anchor, waiting their turn to enter the Panama Canal and cross to the Caribbean. Behind them rise the towers of Panama City. Out in the gulf, the green Pearl Islands earned their name: La Peregrina, one of the most famous pearls in history, was found there in the 16th century.
Q645012.w: A broad Pacific bay with Panama City on its northern shore, ships anchored offshore and a cluster of green islands to the south-east.
f: The canal's Pacific entrance lies at the head of the gulf, next to Panama City.
Surprisingly, the Pacific end of the canal lies farther east than its Atlantic end.
From about July to October humpback whales from the Southern Hemisphere come here to breed.

q.q: Which Panama Canal entrance lies farther east?

Q1974744.t: The western doorway of the Northwest Passage
Q1974744.s: Ships threading the Northwest Passage from the Pacific side enter the Canadian Arctic islands here, between Banks Island to the north and the mainland to the south. Roald Amundsen sailed through in 1905 aboard the little Gjøa, completing the first voyage along the whole passage the following year, and the gulf now bears his name. For most of the year it is covered in ice.
Q1974744.w: A broad arm of the Arctic Ocean between flat Banks Island to the north and the mainland coast, usually white with ice.
f: An area of open water that often stays unfrozen, the Cape Bathurst polynya, forms at its western end.
Bowhead and beluga whales pass through it in summer.
Victoria Island, one of the largest islands in the world, borders it to the east.

q.q: Whose ship first sailed the whole Northwest Passage, via this gulf?

Q5605258.t: An ice-choked sound where Parry won a prize
Q5605258.s: In September 1819 William Parry's ships pushed west into this sound and crossed 110° W, winning a £5,000 reward offered by Parliament for getting that far along the Northwest Passage. Beyond it the ice stopped them. Viscount Melville Sound is still one of the passage's hardest stretches: thick, old sea ice drifts in from the Arctic Ocean and often lingers all summer.
Q5605258.w: A wide channel of white sea ice between Melville Island to the north and Victoria Island to the south.
f: It is named after Viscount Melville, First Lord of the Admiralty at the time.
Parry's crews wintered at Winter Harbour on Melville Island in 1819–1820.
The sound is part of Parry Channel, the main east–west route of the Northwest Passage.

q.q: How much prize money did Parry's crews win for crossing 110° W?

Q1165951.t: An Arctic bay whose tides rival the Bay of Fundy
Q1165951.s: Ungava Bay's tides are contenders for the world record: in Leaf Basin, on its western side, the sea can rise and fall by around 16 m, rivalling the Bay of Fundy. The bay is frozen for much of the year, and floes grind along its shores as the tide lifts and drops them. Kuujjuaq, the largest community in Nunavik, lies up the Koksoak River near its southern end.
Q1165951.w: A broad bay in far northern Quebec opening north into Hudson Strait, with a large, flat-topped island near its mouth.
f: Akpatok Island, in the bay, is ringed by high limestone cliffs where seabirds nest.
Kuujjuaq is the administrative centre of Nunavik, the Inuit region of northern Quebec.
The bay opens into Hudson Strait, the passage between the Atlantic and Hudson Bay.

q.q: Which famous bay's tides do Ungava Bay's tides rival?

Q243125.t: A sea at the top of the world, locked in old ice
Q243125.s: The Lincoln Sea lies at about 83° N, between the northern tips of Ellesmere Island and Greenland, less than 800 km from the North Pole. Its sea ice is among the thickest and oldest in the Arctic, pressed against the coast by the drifting pack. On its shore stands Alert, the northernmost permanently inhabited place on Earth.
Q243125.w: A frozen expanse of jumbled white pack ice, bordered by the dark, mountainous northern coasts of Ellesmere Island and Greenland.
f: Cape Columbia on Ellesmere Island, the northernmost point of Canada, overlooks it.
Greenland's Cape Morris Jesup, near its eastern edge, is among the northernmost points of land on Earth.
Scientists call this region the 'Last Ice Area', expected to keep its summer ice the longest.

q.q: Which settlement on the Lincoln Sea is the northernmost inhabited place?

Q171846.t: The stormy strait that proved Tasmania an island
Q171846.s: Until 1798 Europeans did not know whether Tasmania was joined to the mainland. Then George Bass and Matthew Flinders sailed right around it through this strait, which now bears Bass's name. It is about 240 km wide but shallow, mostly 50 to 70 m deep, so the westerly gales of the Roaring Forties whip up short, steep and dangerous seas.
Q171846.w: A wide stretch of sea between Victoria's coast and Tasmania, dotted with islands: King Island in the west, the Furneaux group in the east.
f: During the last Ice Age the strait was dry land, and people walked from the mainland to Tasmania.
Oil and gas have been produced from platforms in its eastern part since the late 1960s.
Flinders Island, the largest of the Furneaux group, is named after Matthew Flinders.

q.q: Who is Bass Strait named after?

Q1135336.t: An ice-choked strait that trapped McClure's ship
Q1135336.s: Thick, old ice from the Arctic Ocean jams into M'Clure Strait, and ships that try this western route of the Northwest Passage rarely get through. Robert McClure's expedition tried in 1851; his ship Investigator became trapped in the ice of Mercy Bay on Banks Island and had to be abandoned. His men were rescued by sledge from the east — and so became the first to cross the whole passage.
Q1135336.w: A broad channel of white pack ice between the flat north coast of Banks Island and Melville Island.
f: The wreck of HMS Investigator was found in shallow water in Mercy Bay in 2010.
The strait opens west onto the Beaufort Sea and the Arctic Ocean.
It is named after Robert McClure, the Irish-born naval officer who led the expedition.

q.q: Which ship did McClure abandon in the ice near this strait?

Q2328243.t: The blue whales' dining room below a hunchbacked volcano
Q2328243.s: Each summer the largest animals that have ever lived come here to feed: blue whales gather in the Gulf of Corcovado, between Chiloé Island and the Chilean mainland, to eat swarms of krill. The gulf takes its name from the Corcovado volcano on the mainland shore, whose lopsided summit looks like a hunched back. Rain-soaked forest covers almost every slope around it.
Q2328243.w: A wide gulf between the green island of Chiloé and the mountainous mainland, with a snow-capped volcano on the eastern shore.
f: Corcovado volcano rises about 2,300 m above the gulf.
The gulf is one of the most important feeding grounds for blue whales in the Southern Hemisphere.
Chiloé's wooden churches, a UNESCO site, stand on the island's shores to the west.

q.q: What does 'Corcovado' mean in Spanish?

Q281638.t: An Antarctic gulf named after a chewing-gum magnate
Q281638.s: Wrigley Gulf curves along the coast of Marie Byrd Land, in front of the long Getz Ice Shelf, and very few people have ever seen it. An American expedition discovered it in December 1940 and named it after Philip Wrigley, the Chicago chewing-gum manufacturer who had helped fund the venture. Nearby, the huge snowy dome of Mount Siple, a volcano, rises above the ice.
Q281638.w: A broad bay of sea ice and icebergs along the edge of a flat white ice shelf, with a large volcanic dome to the east.
f: The gulf is about 185 km wide.
Mount Siple, on Siple Island nearby, is a volcano more than 3,000 m high.
The Getz Ice Shelf along its shore stretches for hundreds of kilometres.

q.q: Which product made Philip Wrigley's company famous?

Q281737.t: An ice-locked bay named after a New York publisher
Q281737.s: Richard Byrd's expedition flew over this coast of Marie Byrd Land in December 1929 and named the bay after Arthur Hays Sulzberger of The New York Times, a supporter of the venture. Along its shore spreads the Sulzberger Ice Shelf, studded with ice-covered islands and hemmed in by sea ice for most of the year. It remains one of the least visited coasts of the continent.
Q281737.w: A wide bay of white sea ice and ice-shelf edge, dotted with ice-covered islands, along the coast of Marie Byrd Land.
f: The bay was first seen from an aircraft during Byrd's expedition in 1929.
Arthur Hays Sulzberger later became publisher of The New York Times.
Marie Byrd Land, around it, is named after Admiral Byrd's wife.

q.q: Which newspaper is linked to the man Sulzberger Bay honours?

Q898839.t: An Antarctic strait with a ring-shaped volcano
Q898839.s: At the western end of the strait lies a ring-shaped island: Deception Island, a volcano whose flooded crater ships can sail right into through a narrow gap. The Bransfield Strait separates the South Shetland Islands from the icy mountains of the Antarctic Peninsula. It is named after Edward Bransfield, who charted part of the peninsula in January 1820, one of the first sightings of the Antarctic mainland.
Q898839.w: A wide channel between the snowy South Shetland Islands and the glaciated mountains of the Antarctic Peninsula, with a ring-shaped island to the west.
f: The entrance to Deception Island's flooded crater, Neptune's Bellows, is only a few hundred metres wide.
King George Island, on its northern side, hosts research stations of several countries.
Humpback whales feed in the strait in summer.

q.q: What is Deception Island, at the edge of the Bransfield Strait?

Q1056751.t: Antarctica's front door, watched by a smoking volcano
Q1056751.s: Mount Erebus, the southernmost active volcano on Earth, rises 3,794 m above the eastern side of McMurdo Sound, often trailing steam from a lava lake in its crater. Across the water the Dry Valleys lie bare and brown, among the driest places on the planet. The sound is the gateway to the largest research station in Antarctica and to the old routes towards the South Pole.
Q1056751.w: A wide bay of sea ice beside a large island crowned by a smoking volcano, with bare brown valleys in the mountains to the west.
f: Erebus holds one of the few long-lasting lava lakes in the world.
Scott and Shackleton built expedition huts on Ross Island, and several still stand.
James Clark Ross named the sound in 1841 after Archibald McMurdo, an officer of HMS Terror.

q.q: Which active volcano rises over McMurdo Sound?

Q938327.t: A long Arctic sound, once a whalers' winter home
Q938327.s: Cumberland Sound cuts about 250 km into Baffin Island, a broad arm of the sea walled by rugged, glaciated mountains. In the 19th century Scottish and American whalers wintered here, and the remains of a whaling station still stand on Kekerten Island. Today the hamlet of Pangnirtung sits beside a fjord on its north-eastern shore, the gateway to Auyuittuq National Park.
Q938327.w: A long, wide inlet slicing into Baffin Island, lined with snowy mountains and glaciers, often partly covered in sea ice.
f: The old whaling station on Kekerten Island is now a territorial historic park.
Auyuittuq, near Pangnirtung, means 'land that never melts' in Inuktitut.
Beluga whales gather in the sound's waters.

q.q: What does Auyuittuq, the park near Cumberland Sound, mean?

Q1695.t: Where two seas collide at the tip of Denmark
Q1695.s: At Grenen, the sandy northern tip of Denmark, waves from the Skagerrak and the Kattegat run into each other along a line you can stand beside. The Skagerrak itself is a broad channel between Norway's rocky south coast and Jutland, linking the North Sea with the approaches to the Baltic. Along the Norwegian side it plunges to about 700 m, the deepest part of the Norwegian Trench.
Q1695.w: A wide channel between Norway's island-fringed south coast and the flat, sandy tip of Denmark, with Sweden's west coast to the east.
f: The Skagen painters of the late 1800s were drawn to the town by its famous clear light.
The strait is about 240 km long and between about 80 and 140 km wide.
It is one of the busiest shipping routes in Europe.

q.q: Which sea meets the Skagerrak at Grenen?

Q131716.t: The shallow gateway between the North Sea and the Baltic
Q131716.s: Most ships sailing between the Baltic and the open ocean cross the Kattegat, a shallow sea hemmed in by Denmark's Jutland on the west and Sweden's west coast on the east. It averages only about 23 m deep and is dotted with sandbanks and low islands such as Læsø and Anholt. At its southern end it narrows into the Øresund and the Danish belts.
Q131716.w: A shallow, rounded sea between flat Danish shores to the west and Sweden's rocky, island-fringed coast to the east, with Gothenburg in the north-east.
f: Part of Anholt, in the middle of the Kattegat, is a desert-like expanse of dunes and lichen.
Gothenburg, Sweden's second city, stands where the Göta River enters it.
Its water grows fresher towards the south, as brackish Baltic water flows out on the surface.

q.q: Which Swedish city stands on the Kattegat?

Q654010.t: A muddy funnel of huge tides and river mouths
Q654010.s: The Gulf of Khambhat narrows like a funnel into Gujarat, and the tide rushes up it so hard that the range can reach around 10 m, among the largest in India. Four big rivers — the Narmada, Tapi, Mahi and Sabarmati — pour in silt, turning the water an opaque brown. On its western shore at Alang, huge old ships are run aground on the beach to be broken up.
Q654010.w: A long, funnel-shaped gulf of opaque brown water on India's west coast, north of Mumbai and east of the Kathiawar peninsula.
f: Alang is one of the largest ship-breaking yards in the world.
The rising tide can race up the gulf as a tidal bore.
Its old name, the Gulf of Cambay, comes from Khambhat, once a great trading port at its head.

q.q: What happens to ships run aground at Alang?
q.a: They are broken up for scrap
